title: Conservation of Energy
short_intro: The principle of conservation of energy states that the total mechanical energy of an isolated system remains constant if only conservative forces act upon it. It serves as a foundational conservation law derived from the time-translation invariance of physical systems.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Work-energy theorem, conservative and non-conservative forces, conservation of mechanical energy in one-dimensional motion, potential energy curves, and simple harmonic motion applications.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General conservative force fields defined by curl-free conditions (nabla × F = 0), potential energy in three dimensions, central force motion energy integrals, and work-energy relations in rotating or non-inertial frames involving fictitious forces.

prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion and free-body diagrams
Line integrals of vector fields and scalar products
Concept of center of mass and external/internal forces

concept_notes.heading: Conservative Forces and Potential Energy
bullets: A force F is conservative if the work done by it along a closed path is zero: oint F · dr = 0.
The work done by a conservative force is independent of the path taken and depends only on the initial and final positions.
Potential energy U(r) is defined exclusively for conservative forces such that delta U = -W = -int F · dr.

concept_notes.heading: Mechanical Energy Conservation Law
bullets: Total mechanical energy E is the sum of kinetic energy (K) and potential energy (U): E = K + U.
When only conservative forces do work, delta K = -delta U, which implies delta E = delta K + delta U = 0.
In the presence of non-conservative forces like friction (f_k), the change in mechanical energy equals the work done by non-conservative forces: delta E = W_{nc} = -f_k s.

concept_notes.heading: Potential Energy Curves and Equilibrium
bullets: The force is related to the potential energy function by the negative gradient: F(x) = -dU/dx.
Stable equilibrium occurs at local minima of the potential energy curve where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² > 0.
Unstable equilibrium occurs at local maxima where dU/dx = 0 and d²U/dx² < 0, while neutral equilibrium corresponds to a flat region.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Conservation in Central Force Fields
bullets: Central forces (such as gravitational and electrostatic forces) are directed toward a fixed center and are inherently conservative.
For a particle in a central force field, angular momentum L is conserved alongside total energy E, reducing the effective 3D problem to 1D motion.
The effective potential energy includes the centrifugal barrier term: U_{eff}(r) = U(r) + L² / (2mu r²).

derivations.title: Work-Energy Theorem to Conservation of Mechanical Energy
derivations.conditions: Particle of mass m moving under the influence of a conservative force F(x)
steps: Start with Newton's second law: F = m(dv/dt) = m v (dv/dx).
Integrate the force from position x_i to x_f to find work done: W = int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) dx = int_{x_i}^{x_f} m v (dv/dx) dx = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_i^2 = K_f - K_i.
By definition of potential energy for a conservative force, W = U(x_i) - U(x_f) = - (U_f - U_i).
Equating the two expressions for work: K_f - K_i = -(U_f - U_i), which rearranges to K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

derivations.title: Condition for a Force to be Conservative
derivations.conditions: Vector force field F(x, y, z) acting in a simply connected region
steps: Express the work done along an arbitrary path as W = int (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz).
For work to be path-independent, the integrand must be an exact differential, implying F · dr = -dU.
Using Stokes' theorem on a closed loop, oint F · dr = iint (\nabla \times F) · n dA = 0 for any surface bounded by the loop.
For this integral to vanish for all arbitrary surfaces, the integrand must vanish identically throughout the region.

formula_sheet.name: Work-Energy Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: W_{net} = Net work done, m = mass, v_f = final velocity, v_i = initial velocity
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid in both inertial and non-inertial frames if pseudo-forces are included

formula_sheet.name: Relation Between Force and Potential Energy
formula_sheet.variables: F(x) = Conservative force component, U = Potential energy

formula_sheet.name: Three-Dimensional Conservative Force
formula_sheet.equation_html: F = -\nabla U = -\left(\hat{i}\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} + \hat{j}\frac{\partial U}{\partial y} + \hat{k}\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)
formula_sheet.variables: F = Force vector, \nabla = Gradient operator, U = Potential energy scalar field

formula_sheet.name: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
formula_sheet.variables: K = Kinetic energy, U = Potential energy at states 1 and 2

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Potential Energy (Near Earth)
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, g = acceleration due to gravity, h = height above reference level
formula_sheet.conditions: Uniform gravitational field near Earth's surface

formula_sheet.name: Elastic Potential Energy of a Spring
formula_sheet.variables: k = spring constant, x = displacement from natural length

formula_sheet.name: Effective Potential in Central Force Motion
formula_sheet.variables: U(r) = Central potential, L = Angular momentum, \mu = Reduced mass, r = radial distance
formula_sheet.conditions: Central force motion in polar coordinates

formula_sheet.name: Total Mechanical Energy with Non-Conservative Forces
formula_sheet.variables: W_{nc} = Work done by non-conservative forces such as friction or drag

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Energy Curve U(x) vs Position x
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A smooth curve with multiple local minima and maxima, showing a horizontal total energy line E intersecting the curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Regions where E > U(x) represent allowed motion where kinetic energy is positive. Points where E = U(x) are turning points. Local minima indicate stable equilibrium; local maxima indicate unstable equilibrium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions asking to identify equilibrium types, turning points, and maximum velocity positions from graphical data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Simple Pendulum Energy Conservation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar chart or stacked area plot showing kinetic energy and potential energy varying inversely with displacement, while their sum remains constant over one time period.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At the extreme amplitudes, potential energy is at its maximum and kinetic energy is zero. At the mean position, kinetic energy is at its maximum and potential energy is at its reference minimum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems on finding string tension, velocity at the lowest point, and height of swing.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mod Atwood Machine Energy Dissipation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear plot of total mechanical energy versus time for a system experiencing sliding friction, showing a negative slope proportional to the frictional dissipation rate.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The decrease in mechanical energy per unit time directly equals the thermal energy generated by non-conservative friction forces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing isolated conservative systems from dissipative systems in multi-body problems.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 2 kg moves in a conservative force field where the potential energy is given by U(x) = 3x^3 - 6x^2 Joules. Find the force acting on the particle at x = 2 m.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between force and potential energy in 1D: F(x) = -dU/dx.
Differentiate U(x) with respect to x: dU/dx = d/dx (3x^3 - 6x^2) = 9x^2 - 12x.
Substitute x = 2 m into the derivative: dU/dx|_{x=2} = 9(2)^2 - 12(2) = 9(4) - 24 = 36 - 24 = 12 J/m.

solved_numericals.question: A 1 kg block slides down a frictionless track from a height of 5 m and then enters a rough horizontal surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction \mu_k = 0.2. How far will the block travel on the rough surface before coming to rest?
solution_steps: Apply conservation of mechanical energy for the descent to find velocity at the bottom: \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh \implies v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 5} = \sqrt{98} m/s.
Use the work-energy theorem for the motion on the rough surface: \Delta K = W_{nc}.
The final kinetic energy is zero, so 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = -f_k s, where f_k = \mu_k mg.
Substitute the values: \frac{1}{2}m(2gh) = \mu_k mg s \implies mgh = \mu_k mgs.
Cancel mass m and solve for distance s: s = \frac{h}{\mu_k} = \frac{5}{0.2} = 25 m.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass m moves in a central potential U(r) = - \frac{k}{r}. If the particle moves in a circular orbit of radius r_0, find its total mechanical energy in terms of k and r_0.
solution_steps: The centripetal force is provided by the negative derivative of the potential: F(r) = -dU/dr = -\frac{k}{r^2}.
The potential energy at r_0 is U(r_0) = -\frac{k}{r_0}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Macroscopic energy conservation assumes macroscopic bodies where internal quantum states and rest-mass energy conversions remain constant.

Potential energy formulations require forces to be strictly position-dependent and curl-free (conservative); velocity-dependent forces like magnetic Lorentz forces or resistive drag cannot be fully represented by a scalar potential alone.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Friction always violates the conservation of energy law.
common_misconceptions.correct: Friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy, but total energy of the universe remains strictly conserved.
common_misconceptions.why: Mechanical energy is not conserved in dissipative systems, but the total energy including internal thermal energy is always conserved.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Potential energy belongs exclusively to a single object.
common_misconceptions.correct: Potential energy is a property of the configuration of a system of interacting bodies.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravitational or electrostatic potential energy requires at least two interacting masses or charges.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Work done by a conservative force depends on the chosen path if the speed changes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Work done by a conservative force depends solely on the initial and final positions, regardless of path or speed.
common_misconceptions.why: By definition, line integrals of conservative vector fields around any open path depend strictly on endpoints.

quick_revision: Mechanical energy E = K + U is conserved if and only if all working forces are conservative.
Force is the negative spatial derivative of potential energy: F = -dU/dx.
Stable equilibrium exists at local minima of potential energy where d²U/dx² > 0.
